## Why circular motion is special
An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating because its direction changes continuously. Velocity is a vector: change the direction, and you change the velocity. The acceleration that turns the velocity toward the center is called centripetal acceleration; it never changes speed, only direction.
The net force that produces centripetal acceleration is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite. For uniform circular motion (constant speed), the key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = m v²/r, and speed from the period T: v = 2πr/T. The acceleration vector always points from the object toward the center, perpendicular to the velocity.

## Key formulas for uniform circular motion
In uniform circular motion, an object moves at constant speed but still accelerates because its direction changes continuously. This acceleration, called centripetal acceleration, always points toward the center of the circle and never changes the speed, only the direction.
The net force causing this acceleration is the centripetal force, which must be supplied by something real, such as tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite.
The key formulas are: centripetal acceleration a = v²/r, centripetal force F = m v²/r, and speed from the period T (time for one full circle) v = 2πr/T. Units: v in m/s, r in m, a in m/s², F in N, T in s.
Key: The net force that produces it is the centripetal force, and it must be supplied by something real: tension in a string, friction on a tire, or gravity on a satellite.
Key: An object moving in a circle at constant speed is still accelerating, because its direction changes continuously.
Key: Speed from the period T (time for one full circle): v = 2πr / T

Q: What is the direction of the centripetal acceleration vector? A: toward the center. The passage says the acceleration vector always points from the object toward the center of the circle.
Q: A satellite orbits Earth. What supplies the centripetal force? A: Gravity. The passage lists gravity on a satellite as a real source of centripetal force.

## Worked example: car on a flat curve
When a car rounds an unbanked (flat) curve, the only horizontal force that can change its direction is friction between the tires and the road. This friction must point toward the center of the curve to provide the centripetal force needed for circular motion.
In the worked example, a 1200 kg car at 20 m/s on a 50 m radius curve has centripetal acceleration a = v²/r = 8.0 m/s². The required force is F = ma = 9600 N (about 9.6 kN).
If the maximum available friction is less than this required force (e.g., on ice or with worn tires), the car cannot turn sharply enough. It skids outward—not because an outward force pushes it, but because the centripetal force is missing, so the car continues in a straight line (Newton's first law).

Key: Required force = m * (v²/r).
Key: If friction is insufficient, the car skids outward due to lack of centripetal force, not an outward force.

## Worked example: geostationary satellite
A geostationary satellite orbits Earth in a circle with a period of 24 hours, matching Earth's rotation. Its orbital speed is found from the circumference of the orbit divided by the period: v = 2πr / T. For a radius of 4.23 × 10⁷ m and T = 86,400 s, the speed is about 3.1 km/s.
The centripetal acceleration needed to keep it in circular motion is a = v² / r. Plugging in the values gives about 0.22 m/s². This acceleration is provided entirely by Earth's gravity, which pulls the satellite toward the center of the orbit.
The satellite is in free fall—it is continuously falling toward Earth but moving sideways fast enough that it keeps missing. It is not floating without forces; gravity is acting on it, providing the centripetal force that bends its path into a circle.

Centripetal force is not a new kind of force; it is the name for whatever real force (tension, friction, gravity, a normal force) points toward the center. Never draw a 'centripetal force' arrow on a free-body diagram in addition to the actual forces — identify which actual force plays that role.

## Scope and Definitions
This law applies to all residential lease agreements made within the Republic of Ostrava. Key terms are defined: a Tenant is any natural person who occupies a dwelling under a written lease; a Landlord is the legal holder of title or the authorized manager of the premises; and the Regulatory Office is the Office of Tenancy Regulation established under Article 12.
The law sets a minimum lease term of 120 calendar days, unless both parties agree in writing to a shorter term, which cannot be less than 30 days. Any lease shorter than 30 days is void from the start.
Rent can be increased at most once every 12 months. The increase cannot exceed 5% of the prevailing rent, unless the Landlord gets prior written approval from the Housing Arbitration Bureau showing that capital improvements exceeding 15% of the property's assessed value have been completed. This provision will be on the upcoming assessment.
A security deposit cannot exceed two months' rent. It must be held in an escrow account by the Ministry of Urban Dwelling and returned within 45 days after the lease ends, minus lawful deductions for damage beyond normal wear.
The Landlord must keep structural elements, plumbing, heating, and electrical systems in habitable condition. The Tenant must keep the interior clean and promptly notify the Landlord of any defect. If the Landlord fails to fix a reported defect within 14 days, the Tenant can reduce rent by up to 10% per month until it is fixed.
Either party can end a periodic tenancy by giving written notice at least 60 days before the intended termination date.
